subject: history
title: Hitler's rise to power
issue: Why was Hitler able to come to power in Germany by 1933?

sources.provenance: From a Nazi Party election leaflet, 1932.
sources.text: Six million Germans have no work. The parties of the Republic have had fourteen years and have given you hunger. Only one movement promises work and bread. Vote for the man who will make Germany strong again.

sources.provenance: A former factory worker from Berlin, interviewed in the 1970s about the year 1932.
sources.text: I had been out of work for two years. My children were hungry. I did not care much about politics before. The Nazis ran a soup kitchen on my street and their men looked disciplined. I thought, nobody else is doing anything, so let them try.

sources.provenance: From a school textbook by a British historian, 1990s.
sources.text: The Depression gave Hitler his audience, but it did not give him power. In the election of November 1932 the Nazi vote fell. Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 because a small group of conservative politicians persuaded the President to appoint him. They believed they could control him.

sources.provenance: A Social Democrat member of the German parliament, writing in exile in 1934.
sources.text: We and the Communists spent our strength fighting each other in the streets and in parliament. Together we had more seats than the Nazis in November 1932. We never joined hands. The Republic fell because its defenders were divided.

subject: history
title: The Munich Agreement
issue: Was the policy of appeasement a mistake?

sources.provenance: From a British newspaper editorial, 1 October 1938, the day after the Munich Agreement.
sources.text: The Prime Minister has come home with peace. A week ago families were fitting gas masks on their children and trenches were being dug in the parks. Today those children can sleep. No one who remembers the last war will say the price was too high.

sources.provenance: A reader's letter to a British newspaper, October 1938.
sources.text: We have bought a few months of quiet by handing a small country's land to a dictator, without asking that country. He has broken every promise he has made. He will take this as proof that threats work, and he will ask for more.

sources.provenance: A cartoon published in a Soviet newspaper in October 1938, shortly after the Munich Agreement.
sources.text: [The cartoon shows two well-dressed men, labelled 'Britain' and 'France', standing at a signpost. They point a wolf in a German army cap along the road marked 'East'. Behind them lies a torn map of Czechoslovakia.]

sources.provenance: From a history book written in the 1990s.
sources.text: In 1938 Britain's air defences were not ready. Radar stations covered only part of the coast and few modern fighter planes were in service. By September 1939 both had been greatly strengthened. Whatever its other effects, the year gained at Munich was used.

subject: history
title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
issue: Who gained more from the Cuban Missile Crisis?

sources.provenance: From an American news magazine, November 1962.
sources.text: The Soviet ships turned back. The missiles are being crated and shipped home under the eyes of American aircraft. The President stood firm, and the other side gave way. It is a clear victory for the United States.

sources.provenance: From a Soviet newspaper, November 1962.
sources.text: The Soviet government has saved the peace of the world. Our missiles were sent to protect Cuba from invasion. The United States has now promised not to invade. Cuba is safe, so the missiles are no longer needed there.

sources.provenance: From a history textbook, 2000s.
sources.text: Publicly, the Soviet Union removed its missiles from Cuba and the United States promised not to invade the island. Secretly, the United States also agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey some months later. This part of the deal was kept from the public for many years.

sources.provenance: A Cuban official, recalling the crisis in an interview in the 1990s.
sources.text: We learned from the radio that the missiles were leaving. Nobody in Moscow asked us. The two great powers settled the matter over our heads, and we were left feeling like a piece on their board.

subject: history
title: The Marshall Plan
issue: Was the Marshall Plan an act of generosity?

sources.provenance: The narration of an American government information film shown in Western Europe, 1949.
sources.text: Two years ago this bakery in France had no flour. Today the ovens are lit again. The wheat came by ship, a gift from the American people to free people who wish to stay free.

sources.provenance: From a Soviet newspaper, 1947.
sources.text: The dollar is being used as a weapon. Countries that accept this so-called aid must open their markets to American goods and take orders from Washington. It is a plan to buy Europe.

sources.provenance: From a history textbook, 2000s.
sources.text: Between 1948 and 1952 the United States gave about 13 billion dollars to sixteen European countries. The Soviet Union refused the aid and made the countries of Eastern Europe refuse it too. Much of the money was spent on American goods.

sources.provenance: A poster printed in Western Europe with Marshall Plan funds, 1950.
sources.text: [The poster shows a windmill whose four blades are the flags of European countries, turning in a wind marked 'Co-operation'.] Caption: 'Together we rebuild.'

questions.question: What does Source A tell you about how the United States wanted Europeans to see the Marshall Plan? Explain your answer.
questions.model: The United States wanted Europeans to see the Plan as generous help with nothing asked in return. The film calls the wheat 'a gift from the American people'. A gift is free, so viewers are led to feel grateful, not suspicious. It also ties the aid to people 'who wish to stay free', so accepting it looks like choosing the American side.

questions.question: How reliable is Source B about the aims of the Marshall Plan? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is partly reliable. B claims that countries 'must open their markets to American goods'. Source C supports part of this: 'Much of the money was spent on American goods', so the United States did gain. But C gives no support to B's claim that countries would 'take orders from Washington'. B is also a Soviet newspaper in 1947, when the Soviet Union was refusing the aid and making Eastern Europe refuse it. It needed its readers to see the Plan as a trap, so it uses words like 'weapon' and 'buy Europe'. It is reliable for the Soviet view, and only partly for the Plan's aims.

questions.question: Why was Source D printed? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It says European countries will recover only if they work together. The blades are different flags, but they turn as one windmill in a wind marked 'Co-operation', and the caption says 'Together we rebuild'. It is aimed at ordinary people in Western Europe, where it was printed. It was paid for with Marshall Plan funds in 1950, when the United States wanted the countries it was helping to trade with each other and stand together against communism. So it wants viewers to support co-operation between their countries, and to think well of the Plan behind it.

subject: history
title: The Treaty of Versailles
issue: Was the Treaty of Versailles fair to Germany?

sources.provenance: From a German newspaper, June 1919.
sources.text: The victors have written this treaty without us and now order us to sign. We must give up land, our army and our colonies, and accept the blame for a war that all the powers stumbled into. This is not peace. It is a sentence.

sources.provenance: From a French newspaper, June 1919.
sources.text: For four years the war was fought on our soil. Our mines were flooded and our villages are rubble. Germany's own towns were never touched. It is only just that the country which caused the ruin should pay to repair it.

sources.provenance: From a history textbook, 2000s.
sources.text: Germany lost about 13 per cent of its land and its army was cut to 100,000 men. Yet Germany itself had forced a far harsher peace on Russia in March 1918. Germany remained the largest economy on the continent after 1919.

sources.provenance: A British soldier stationed in Germany, in a letter home, 1919.
sources.text: The people here are thin and the shops are bare. They ask how they can ever pay what is demanded. I fought them for three years, but I do not see how making them hopeless will keep the peace for our children.

questions.question: How different are Sources A and B? Explain your answer.
questions.model: They differ on whether the treaty was fair. A says 'This is not peace. It is a sentence.' B says it is 'only just' that Germany should pay. They are similar in showing that Germany was made to carry the cost of the war. A says Germany must 'accept the blame' and give up land, and B says Germany 'should pay to repair' the ruin. They also differ in whose side they take. A speaks for Germans, who had no say, so it stresses that the treaty was written 'without us'. B speaks for the French, who suffered the fighting, so it stresses 'our villages are rubble'.

questions.question: How useful is Source A in helping you understand whether the Treaty of Versailles was fair? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is useful. It shows why Germans thought the treaty unfair: it was written 'without us' and they had to 'accept the blame' for the war. It is limited. It lists only Germany's losses and does not compare them with anything. Source C shows that Germany 'had forced a far harsher peace on Russia' and 'remained the largest economy on the continent'. A is also a German newspaper in the month of signing, written to share its readers' anger. So it is very useful for how Germans felt, but not for judging whether the terms were in fact unfair.

questions.question: 'The Treaty of Versailles was unfair to Germany.' Using the sources, explain how far you would agree with this statement.
questions.model: Source A supports the statement: Germany had to give up 'land, our army and our colonies' and take the blame, with no say. Source D supports it too: the soldier meets people who 'ask how they can ever pay what is demanded'. Source B disagrees. The war was fought on French soil while Germany's towns 'were never touched', so it is 'only just' that Germany pays. Source C also disagrees: Germany 'had forced a far harsher peace on Russia' and was still 'the largest economy on the continent'. The sources that disagree are stronger. A and B each speak for their own country. D is a former enemy with no reason to pity Germans, so his worry is believable, but he judges by what he sees in one place. C is written long after, with the figures, and it measures the treaty against what Germany itself did. So I agree only to a small extent: the treaty was harsh and felt unfair, but by the standards of the time it was not.
